In bisyllabic words the stress is always on the first syllable, while in trisyllabic words the word stress in on the penultimate syllable . pa'naqeng ka'nayong In the case of compounds, the same rules apply as for the constituent components, although this manifests itself as primary and secondary stress, with primary stress being placed on the final lexeme . anen ' mengar nariq ' edang ai ' waq a ' in 3.4 . new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable: the first syllable of disyllables (about 95% of the lexicon per Samely 1991 §2.3.1) and the middle syllable of trisyllables; monosyllables are stressed. Compounds keep the stress of each member, with primary stress on the final member and secondary stress on the preceding one(s).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Only in compounds: non-final lexemes carry secondary stress, the final lexeme primary stress (Samely & Barnes 2013: 16). Samely 1991 §2.3.1 gives the same for tebeq 'mader 'sit for a long time': 'the first element receives secondary stress while primary stress lies on the second element', and compounds have two word stresses versus one in simplex forms.
new_statements.exceptions: None for simplex words ('entirely regular'). Samely 1991 §2.3.1 notes that some trisyllabic loanwords do not always conform to Kedang syllable structure; an Anthropos (2005) review snippet cites Samely 1991: 101 for stress reversal distinguishing some compounds from phrases (a black 'bird vs a 'blackbird type) — not verified on the page.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (citation forms in a dictionary introduction); compound stress treated separately. Quoted from Google Books snippet feed responses (saved XML), not from the full page; the deciding sentences came back identically across eight independent queries, but the page itself was not opened (Brill and Google Books HTML viewer refuse our network).
new_statements.identity_note: Kedang proper (keda1252 / ksx), north-eastern Lembata; Fricke 2019 labels Samely's data 'KD-Leuwayang' (Leuwayang village variety) and Samely & Barnes 2013 covers the same material. No dialect split is given in Glottolog; the statement is presented by the authors as valid for Kedang as a whole.
